OVERVIEW OF THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND The University had its beginning as the State Agricultural School chartered in 1888.
The federal Morrill Act of 1862 provided the framework within which the school became the land-grant institution of the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) and in 1892, the school became the Rhode Island College of Agricultural and Mechanic Arts.
The first class of 17 members was graduated two years later.

In 1909 the name of the College was changed to Rhode Island State College and the program of study was revised and expanded.
In 1951, the college became known as the University of Rhode Island by act of the State’s General Assembly.
The Universit y of Rhode Island is the S tate’s flagship land and sea grant research institution, with a commitment to urban initiatives.
A student-centered research institution, URI actively partners with other organizations globally and locally to advance knowledge and to develop informed residents and leaders.
URI is committed to high -quality education, community engagement, and solving the world’s most important challenges.
Situated on the traditional land and territories of the Narragansett Nation and the Niantic People, URI strives to create a diverse and inclusive environment for researchers, teachers, learners, and community members.

URI’s Strategic Plan, Focus URI 2023-2033, lays out the strategic vision for the University for the next decade, outlining four strategic priorities and the actions the University will take to achieve them: Strategic Priority 1: Broaden the University’s impact through a reinvigorated commitment to its land- and sea-grant missions and the State of Rhode Island Strategic Priority 2: Enhance student achievement by cultivating an engaged and inclusive learning environment Strategic Priority 3: Foster an inclusive, people-centered culture Strategic Priority 4: Implement leading-edge administrative and financial systems and practices to power the University of the future

A-3 The University’s main campus in Kingston, RI encompasses approximately 1,400 acres in Kingston, 30 miles south of Providence in the northeastern metropolitan corridor between New York and Boston.
The 165-acre Narragansett Bay Campus (the “Bay Campus”), located six miles to the east overlooking the west passage of the Narragansett Bay, is home to the Graduate School of Oceanography , and the Ocean Engineering Department of the College of Engineering, and the College of Environment and Life Sciences.
In Providence, the University offers degree programs and non- credit courses and workshops in various locations.
In the western section of the State, 20 miles from Kingston, the 2,300 acres of woods, fields, streams and ponds on the W.
Alton Jones Campus are the site of research by various principal investigators.
The University offers degree programs through the doctoral level.
The University had a combined graduate, undergraduate and dual high school enrollment headcount of 14,452 students for the f all 2024 official reporting.
First year applications for fall 2024 were once again at record levels with 25,391 applications.

GOVERNANCE The Board of Governors for Higher Education became the governing body for the University in 1981, until the Board of Education assumed governance in January 2013.
In 2014, the Board of Education created two councils, including the Council on Postsecondary Education (the “Council”) which exercised oversight of the University, Rhode Island College (“RIC”) and the Community College of Rhode Island (“CCRI”).
On February 1, 2020, governance of the University was transferred to the newly constituted Board of Trustees for the University of Rhode Island (the “Board of Trustees” or the “URI Board”), whose purpose is the oversight of the University .
The Board of Education and the Council continue to provide oversight for RIC and CCRI .
The URI Board assumed all the powers and duties with respect to the University formerly assigned to the Board of Education and the Council.
The State continues to oversee State funding of higher education, approve borrowing and drive education policy.
The University is held to meeting performance measures required by the State.

The new organizational structure for URI did not materially change the funding or financing arrangements of the State's three publ ic higher education institutions , except in that the URI Board of Trustees has final approval of tuition and mandatory fee rates .
The new URI Board continues to share responsibility for its portion of previously issued bonds for the State ’s colleges, which include debt issued by all three public higher institutions in the State: URI, Rhode Island College and the Community College of Rhode Island.
The enabling legislation creating the Board of Trustees is codified in Rhode Island General Laws Title 16, Chapter 32.
The Trustees were originally appointed with staggered terms to ensure continuity on the Board.
On an annual basis, trustees are considered for appointment and reappointment by the Governor and are confirmed by the State legislature by the end of each legislative session, typically by June.
Three-year terms will again be staggered, as shown by the term expiration dates of those Trustees who have been reappointed to date.

The Faculty Senate was authorized in 1960 by the general faculty to conduct any business assigned to the faculty by law or by the Rhode Island Board of Education/Council on Postsecondary Education and now by the Board of Trustees .
The Graduate Council is the representative body for the graduate faculty and determines the academic policies for graduate study.

RESEARCH – GRANTS AND CONTRACTS In fiscal year 2025, the University of Rhode Island received $144.4 million in extramural grants and contracts.
These externally funded activities are aligned with and support the University’s strategic plan, advancing its core missions of research, instruction, service, and economic development as Rhode Island’s flagship public research university.
URI’s research enterprise supports strategic priorities that incl ude academic excellence, student success, workforce development, and engagement with the State of Rhode Island.
Sponsored research spans a broad range of disciplines, including engineering, health, environmental studies, social sciences, the arts, and ocean and marine sciences.
These activities enhance academic programs and provide structured experiential learning opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, including laboratory and field research, interdisciplinary work, and creative scholarship.

A core component of URI’s research profile is its long standing leadership in ocean science, coastal resilience, and the Blue Economy , which aligns with institutional strategic priorities and statewide economic development goals.
Through its Graduate School of Oceanography, College of the Environment and Life Sciences, College of Engineering and affiliated research centers, URI serves as a hub for ocean and marine research, workforce training, and technology development.
The University hosts and suppor ts ocean observing systems, marine instrumentation development, underwater systems research, and data analytics that are relevant to environmental monitoring, national security, fisheries, and offshore infrastructure.
These activities position URI as a key academic partner for federal agencies, industry, and regional stakeholders engaged in ocean and maritime technologies.
Research funding is derived from a diversified portfolio of federal agencies, state sources, private foundations, and industry sponsor s, supporting financial stability and mitigating reliance on any single funding source.

URI’s research enterprise benefits from sustained participation in multi institutional consortia that enhance research capacity and infrastructure.
For example, the University serves as the long standing home institution for the Rhode Island IDeA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence (RI INBRE), a statewide consortium focused on strengthening biomedical research capacity and expanding student training opportunities across Rhode Island’s public and private institutions of higher education.
URI also serves as the lead and coordinating institution for Rhode Island’s National Science Foundation Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) E CORE progra m.
The Rhode Island EPSCoR E CORE Inclusive Network for Excellence in Science and Technology (RII NEST) is designed to strengthen research infrastructure and workforce capacity statewide while promoting equitable, use inspired research.
EPSCoR programming supports undergraduate research and training in laboratory and field methods, data analytics, and scientific communication, aligning with the University’s strategic emphasis on talent development and retention.

Consistent with its land grant and sea grant missions, URI conducts federally funded research addressing environmental, coastal, and public health challenges of direct relevance to Rhode Island and the region.
One such initiative is the Sources, Transport, Exposure and Effects of PFAS (STEEP) projec t, funded by the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences.
STEEP research examines environmental pathways and human health impacts of poly and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) while disseminating findings to inform prevention and mitigation strategies.

A-9 URI’s research activities are integrated into instruction, mentorship, and public engagement, reinforcing strategic goals related to student learning and community impact.
Faculty research informs curricula, honors programs, and public academic programming, including the University’s Honors Colloquium, as well as a wide range of lectures, exhibitions, and performances.
These activities support student outcomes and strengthen URI’s role as a public research resource for the State of Rhode Island.

A-12 Center for Career and Experiential Education The University of Rhode Island’s Center for Career and Experiential Education (“CCEE”), part of the Kent and Diane Fannon Institute for Student Success , engages undergraduate students and alumni in a personal and professional educational experience, from admission through employment.
The Center values its relationships with local and national employer partners and seeks to find innovative ways to connect students, alumni, faculty, and employers in the career education and development process.
The team of Career Education Specialists (“CES”) offer individual and group professional development sessions and on-line modules for students and alumni.
The topics include self -assessments to discover one’s strengths, job and internship searching, networking and brand development strategies, resume and cover letter development, salary negotiation, interviewing skills, and major to career industry clusters.
The highest impact practice involves engaging in opportunities and courses which include relevant connections between coursework, the community and the workforce.

CCEE offers service learning and internship courses to explore a variety of occupations and gain practical experience th rough an internship or civic engagement.
The Employer Relations team develops relationships with local and national employers to connect students and alumni with their desired industries.
This is done through the Rhody Alumni Mentoring (“RAM”) program, car eer and volunteer fairs, networking events, on- campus interviewing, job, internship and volunteer posting, and professional development week.
Rhode Island Inter-institutional Exchange Full-time students matriculated at one of the public institutions of h igher education in Rhode Island may enroll for a maximum of eight credits of their full-time schedule per semester for study at one of the other public institutions at no additional expense.
Each institution will determine and maintain the integrity of the degree to be awarded.
The University has a robust system of transfer and prior-approved courses, along with articulation agreements with the Community College of Rhode Island and other feeder institutions.

Study Abroad The Office of International Education & National Student Exchange promotes the internationalization of education and building of students’ cross -cultural global skills through educational opportunities in a variety of global environments and institutional linkages.
While international education was curtailed in the spring of academic year 2020 and fall and spring of academic year 2021 due to the pandemic, the University has resumed international education and exchanges beginning in 2022- 2023.
Participation rates in 2025- 2026 are approaching pre-pandemic levels across the study abroad portfolio.
In a normal year the University offers over 140 study abroad options in more than 43 countries worldwide through URI sponsored programs and global affiliations; off-campus credit bearing experiences exist for students in all academic disciplines.
The wide array of learning experiences managed by the office support the institutional objective of expanding the global learning opportunities available to the student body and promoting the institutional objective of ensuring that all students are exposed to global perspectives and building global competency skills.

Options beyond traditional classroom learning are available.
These include international internships, research, field study, virtual engagements and other experiential learning opportunities such as ship-based research voyages.
Semester and short-term programs during the Winter J-Term session, Spring Break, and Summer Session programs are available each academic year.
The office also provides comprehensive advising and programming services – from program selection to predeparture preparation and reentry programming – to support student success in all aspects of the education abroad process and context.
In a concerted effort to increase accessibility and affordability, student assistance in securing local and national scholarship awards is provided and developing quality cost-effective study options is given precedence.

Army ROTC is an elective curriculum that students take along with their required college classes.

Army ROTC also offers students the opportunity to earn two- , three-, and four -year scholarships covering full tuition and fees, book money, and a monthly allowance.

Military Science and Leadership is an elective course of study and students can participate during their freshman and sophomore years without any obligation to join the Army.
Marine and Environment-Related Programs Outstanding scholarship in marine science and oceanography at the University dates to the mid-1930s.
Over the past three decades, this strong emphasis on marine studies has extended to environmental topics, developing into an array of undergraduate programs in the natural, physical, and social sciences.
There are more than two dozen majors wi th a marine or environmental focus offered by URI’s colleges, including landscape architecture, physics and physical oceanography, ocean engineering, civil engineering, aquaculture and fishery technology, biological sciences, cell and molecular biology, environmental and natural resource economics, environmental science and management, geology and geological oceanography, marine affairs, marine biology, plant science, sustainable agriculture and food systems, and wildlife and conservation biology.
Several o f the majors are offered jointly with the Graduate School of Oceanography.

Undergraduates are encouraged to explore opportunities at the Narragansett Bay Campus for active participation in the oceanographic sciences.
Juniors and seniors may take classes at the University’s Bay Campus pursuing their individual marine interests, for which they receive full academic credit.
They may also work as part of a research team in the laboratory and in the field under the direct guidance of the Graduate School of Oceanography faculty.
Center for Student Leadership Development To enhance the mission of the University of Rhode Island, the Center for Student Leadership Development aims to provide developmental opportunities for all students to become informed, inclusive, effective, and ethical leaders in the global marketplace thr ough the implementation of learner -centered academic, experiential, and co-curricular programming.
In addition, the Center engages in research, assessment, and advancement in order to positively impact the expanding field of leadership studies.
Through the College of Business, URI offers a minor in Leadership Studies that is customized for each student.

The program uses a cross-disciplinary approach to leadership education designed to complement a student’s academic studies.
All courses utilize a variety of teaching methods but ultimately include some form of experiential learning, practical application, and reflective learning.
LIBRARIES The University libraries include the Robert L.
Carothers Library and Learning Commons (Kingston Campus) and the Claiborn e Pell Marine Science Library (Narragansett Bay Campus).
Collectively, the libraries hold more than 1.3 million bound volumes, 750,000 government publications, 30,000 print

A-14 journals as well as providing online access to more than 169,000 full text journals, 1,750,361 e-books, and over 300 online databases.
Holdings of AV materials, manuscripts, archives, maps, nautical charts and microforms amount to nearly 2.3 million additional items.
The institutional repository, DigitalCommons@URI, provides universal ac cess to scholarly products from URI students and faculty, including open access to prepublication versions of scholarly work as well as digital copies of theses and dissertations.
Currently, DigitalCommons@URI holds 40,584 items.
The University Libraries worked with NOAA to ensure that physical research materials from the National Sea Grant Library are preserved and distributed to interested regional institutions nationwide.
More importantly, the University Libraries worked with the Internet Archive to ensure the entire collection would be digitized by them and made available for scholars throughout the world.
The University Libraries have also been designated as a preservation steward for all NOAA publications.

Staffed by forty faculty and staff, the Unive rsity Libraries offer a range of library services and spaces to complement the teaching, learning, and research mission of URI.
Library faculty lead sections of undergraduate information literacy courses, helping students fulfill core student learning outcomes.
Library staff ensure the accessibility of collections and study spaces to the University Community 99.5 hours per week during regular semesters, and a portion of the Carothers Library is open to support student learning 24/7.
Technical Services faculty and staff ensure the discoverability of and access to books, articles, and other essential research materials through materials acquisition, metadata creation and database maintenance.
Public Services faculty provide information research consultations, programmatic instruction, and point-of-need support for researchers of all levels at the Research Help Desk.

Collaborating with offices and colleges across campus, the Library Innovation Labs consisting of a Makerspace, XR Lab, AV Lab and Knit/Wear Lab offer access to and assistance with advanced technologies, while the Launch Lab highlights solution- and entrepreneurship-focused learning.
The library also hosts URI’s Department of Information Technology Services (ITS) Service Desk, ITS’s Teaching and Lear ning Services, the Academic Innovation Center, the University’s Active Learning Classroom, the Artificial Intelligence Lab, and functions of the Academic Enhancement Center.
The University Libraries are active participants in the following consortia/associations: Association of College and Research Libraries, Consortium of Rhode Island Academic Research Libraries (CRIARL), BLC (Boston Library Consortium), Higher Education Library Information Network (HELIN), EAST (Eastern Academic Scholars’ Trust), ELUNA (Ex Libris Users of North America), ICPSR (Inter - university Consortium for Political and Social Research), HathiTrust, Northeast Research Libraries Consortium (NERL), Lyrasis, OCLC, ORCID and Libraries of Rhode Island (LORI).

As a full member of the Boston Library Consortium (BLC), the University Libraries are part of a network of academic and research libraries in New England.
The BLC focuses on providing high- quality and cost-effective sharing of print, digital and electronic content across member librari es, and acts as an incubator for initiatives relevant to academic and research libraries in the 21st century.

The University conducts a yearly comprehensive admissions marketing program to attract and enroll a diverse, academically qualified student body.
The University of Rhode Island participates each year in more than 490 college fairs, as well as more than 1800 individual high school visits.
With the number of high school graduates on the decline in Rhode Island and the Northeast, the University’s recru itment efforts continue to expand into new domestic and international areas.
In-person recruitment as well as many web and social media platforms and AI are employed to help recruit students.

A-21 ACCESS AND AFFORDABILITY The University has developed a comprehensive enrollment management approach to foster access and affordability while also enhancing selectivity, quality, and student success.
These efforts include, but are not limited to, expansive recruitment strategies, predictive modeling, and an in vestment in financial aid.
These efforts have resulted in record applications and strong enrollments over the past 10 years, with a minor decline in new students that happened during the new FAFSA roll-out in Fall 2024.
A quick rebound in new student enrol lment occurred for Fall 2025.
Student diversity, selectivity and quality have all improved each year.
Because of the University’s mission, the admissions policy is "selective" in that only students deemed prepared for university-level study are granted regular admission.
Due to Rhode Island’s size and declining number of high school graduates, the University enrolls a significant number of students from outside of Rhode Island.
Feedback from families that choose URI is that the University offers quality programs in a safe location at a good cost and value.

As part of the drive for accessibility and affordability, and recognizing the increasing educational diversity of potential students, the University maintains several programs for special populations and has started several new initiatives as well.
The University has worked to keep its tuition and fee rates affordable and competitive.
In addition to its traditional menu of financial aid programs, the University has the following special programs aimed at increasing access and affordability: Talent Development The Talent Development Program (“TD”) recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds.
Students admitted to TD have taken the required core academic courses in high school.
However, the average academic profile for students accepted to the TD program is not the average academic profile for students accepted through the regular admission process.
TD requires an intensive summer academic program prior to the start of the fall semester.
During the TD Summer Program students take university courses and live on campus.

TD students who successfully complete the TD Summer Program continue their enrollment at URI in the fall.
TD students receive academic and individual support from TD Advisors and mentors, and most receive the need based Hardge/Forleo Grant.
To be considered for the TD Program, students apply for admission to URI indicating their interest in TD, and then are considered through a competitive review process.

A-22 Academic Enhancement Center Part of the newly established Fannon Institute for Student Success, the Academic Enhancement Center (“AEC”) supports student learning and academic success through scaffolding student engagement with course content, helping with the development of metacognitive strategies and skills, critical thinking, writing, time management, and test taking skills.
AEC programs are primarily peer -to-peer, enabling the Center to support the development of collaborative learning skills for all students, as well as teaching and leadership skills for student staff.
The AEC offers unique resources including three forms of tutoring in the STEM disciplines; an Academic Skills Development programming, including UCS 160; and the Writing Center for helping students at all levels of writing skills development.
The mission of the Academic Enhancement Center is to help students invest in their academic success.
The AEC learning support programs and services empower students to become more skillful and successful.

The AEC is committed to responding to student needs, collaborating with faculty and providing professional development for the student staff with the goal of enhancing student learning.
Pell Summer Promise Program In an effort to support Pell students in completing their education in a timely manner, URI launched the Pell Summer Promise Program using Federal Pell support and URI aid to help our most needy in- State students take free summer courses.
The goal is to enhance their time to degree and make college more affordable.
COMMUNITY, EQUITY AND DIVERSITY The Office of Community, Equity and Diversity leads institution- wide initiatives to anchor inclusion in every aspect of the University of Rhode I sland’s community and operations.
To advance inclusive excellence, the Office convenes the University Diversity Council, with representatives from every University constituency; curates community education and development opportunities; conducts climate surveys; and, co-hosts with the Office of the President an annual Inclusive Excellence Awards ceremony recognizing faculty, student, staff and community partners’ efforts to foster an inclusive, people -centered culture.

In addition to coordinating the work of diversity professionals embedded in the University’s academic colleges and administrative divisions, the Office of Community, Equity and Diversity oversees four centers that host community development, engagement, celebration, and outreach programs for the entire University: Center for Military and Veteran Education The Center for Military and Veteran Education supports prior, present, and future military -connected students, faculty, and staff as they further their educational and professional objectives.
The Center assists in the transition from military life into student life and beyond and helps veterans connect with the resources and networks of support available to them at URI and within the local community.
Gender and Sexuality Center The URI Gender and Sexuality Center encourages students, faculty, and staff to explore and affirm their multiple and intersecting identities, especially surrounding gender and sexuality.
Through education, advocacy, and community- building, the Gender and Sexuality Center strives to cultivate an inclusive campus culture that celebrates all genders and sexual identities.
The Center provides intersectional programming and collaborates with student leaders and campus partners to strengthen community and

A-23 foster belonging, all while nurturing a student -centered environment that supports academic and personal growth.
Multicultural Student Services Center The URI Multicultural Student Services Center is dedicated to developing a supportive and inclusive campus culture across the boundaries of culture, identity, and discipline.
Celebrating unity in diversity, the Multicultural Center invites all students, faculty, staff, administrators, alumni, and other friends to join in its work in creating a community of learners wi thin and beyond URI.
The URI Multicultural Center collaboratively provides programs and resources that engage, connect and support the URI community in becoming just and culturally competent global citizens.
It also houses The Center for Nonviolence and Peace Studies which promotes and studies approaches to addressing conflict through nonviolence.
Women’s Center The URI Women’s Center partners with others in the URI community to provide an empowering space which promotes social justice for every member of the community, regardless of gender, gender identity, body, ability, sexual orientation, race, spirituality, and ethnicity.

Community members are encouraged to engage and foster continual dialogue on gender and issues that disproportionately affect women a nd their allies.
The URI Women’s Center supports all University students, faculty and staff in expanding their positive potential, agency and life experience.
STUDENT SERVICES Auxiliary Services Auxiliary services consist of housing, dining, student union, and health services which depend on restricted fees and related revenues derived from student clients.
These operations are required by State law to be fully self-supporting.
Undergraduate Housing On-campus residence halls are available to eligib le students during the regular academic year and winter inter-session, with additional availability during the summer.
The University offers a variety of living accommodations with twenty seven residence halls and two apartment complexes.
The residence hal ls include twenty -two traditional residence halls, of which fifteen primarily house first -year residents in Living and Learning Communities, and three undergraduate apartment -style facilities, including the new Brookside apartment -style residence hall comp leted in January 2020.

There are also two International Engineering Program Houses managed by the College of Engineering.
First-year students are strongly encouraged to live on campus other than in exceptional circumstances; in the Fall of 2025 approximately 92% of URI first-year students live in residence halls.
During the Fall 2025 semester, 591 University students reside in the fraternity/sorority system which sponsors 16 sororities and fraternities (the “Greek” houses) located on university land but not owned or operated by the University.
The staff of the Office of Greek Life in the Memorial Union/Student Involvement Department advise these groups.
The Greek houses promote scholarship, citizenship and small group living.
Purchasing and business management for these houses is provided by a private non- profit corporation controlled by the fraternity and sorority members.
In addition, students occupied two specialty houses for Engineering Students operated by the College of Engineering.
Another choice ava ilable to students is living "down the line" in rented rooms or houses near the University in the ocean-side resort areas.

For the Fall 2025 semester, 5,664 undergraduates were resident in on- campus (HRL) facilities on the Kingston campus.
Approximately 56% of URI undergraduate residents were first year students.
In Fall 2025, approximately 57% of undergraduates lived off campus in nearby communities or commuted from home.

The CCEE engages undergraduate students and alumni in a high quality personal and professional educational experience, from admission through employment.
The University has relationships with local and national employer partners and seeks to find innovative ways to connect students, alumni, faculty, and employers in the career education and development process.
Counseling Services.
The Counseling Center is s taffed by licensed mental health counselors, psychologists, and social workers.
The Center offers individual counseling and a variety of skill -building and support groups to help undergraduate and graduate students achieve their academic and life goals.
The Counseling Center provides assistance to students in areas such as adjusting to college life, coping with stress, building satisfying relationships, planning for the future, and coping with anxiety depression, substance use, or other mental health challenges.
The University partners with Telus Health to provide free, confidential, emotional health and wellbeing support, including access to clinicians 24/7 virtually, by phone or chat.
University Chaplains.

The University chaplains are active in providing religious services as well as counseling, advising campus groups, teaching, and programming.
Faith groups include Buddhism, Catholic Center, Chabad, Congregational/UCC, Episcopal Ministry, Jewish Center, Muslim Center, Rhody Christian Fellowship, Sojourn Collegiate Ministry, Unitarian Universalist, and United Methodist. ;.
The chaplains work together to foster dialogue, understanding, and respect among people of different faiths and traditions.
Memorial Union.
The center for campus programs and activities, the Memorial Union houses a wide variety of education, social and cultural services and facilities for undergraduate and graduate students.
These include the Student Entertainment Committee and Student Senate, many student organization offices, the Center for Student Leadership Development (an academic piece that offers a minor as well as peer education opportunities), staff that assist with room scheduling and an information desk.
Student Involvement staff are available to student leaders to provide advising and education in addition to assisting with the planning for their student organization’s events.
Health Services.

University Health Services provides primary ambulatory care to students.
Nurse practitioners and physicians see students by appointment Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. as well as Saturday and Sundays and most holidays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.
Health Services provides laboratory, radiology, and pharmacy services for URI students.
Specialists in gynecology and psychiatry hold regular

A-25 clinics at the Potter Building.
Health Promotion provides education to students on health and wellness issues that support student success while in college and throughout their lifetime.
Violence Prevention and Advocacy Services are a part of the Heal th Services providing awareness, education, and support for survivors of sexual violence and Alcohol and other Drug Education provide comprehensive education, training and support on substance use and prevention.
A travel/immunization clinic administers va ccines available from the pharmacy.
Care provided at Health Services is billed to insurance companies.
The Dean of Students Office.
Staff provide a range of services for students, staff, and faculty focused on student success.
These services include Disability, Access, Inclusion Services for Students, Outreach and Intervention, the Office of Community Standards, Greek Life, and the Office of Commuter Affairs.
The Dean of Students is responsible for leading the university -wide Behavior Intervention Tea m and the Assistant Director of Outreach and Intervention leads the Students of Concern Team.
Staff frequently provide training to faculty and are available for consultation.

Talent Development.
Talent Development recruits and serves Rhode Island high school graduates with college potential who come from historically disadvantaged backgrounds .
Talent Development enrolls approximately 1,100 students annually and its mission is grounded in the University’s mission of enriching students' lives through its land, sea and urban grant traditions. (See “Talent Development” under “Access and Affordability”).
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY SERVICES The University’s Information Technology Services organization (“ITS”) provides leadership, governance, and strategic direction for the technology and enterprise systems that support the University of Rhode Island community.
ITS is responsible for the reliability, security, and ongoing modernization of systems that support instruction, research, administration, and daily University operations.
ITS supports core institutional systems used across the University, including the Learning Management System for online and in-person instruction; enterprise administrative systems supporting student records, human resources, and financial o perations; and centralized support services through the University Help Desk.

ITS also operates and maintains the University’s high-speed network infrastructure, which connects URI campuses to one another and to national and global research networks throug h secure, multi-gigabit fiber-optic connectivity.
During the past year, the University expanded its research computing and artificial intelligence capabilities through the launch of the Institute for AI and Computational Research.
The Institute coordinates advanced computing, artificial intelligence, and data -intensive research activities across the University and strengthens URI’s participation at the Massachusetts Green High Performance Computing Center (MGHPCC), increasing available computing capacity, resilience, and access to shared regional infrastructure.
ITS provides artificial intelligence and research computing infrastructure not only for URI, but for nearly all public and private institutions of higher education in Rhode Island, excluding Brown University.
These services support the University of Rhode Island, Rhode Island College, Community College of Rhode Island, Bryant University, Salve Regina University, and other partner institutions.

This shared infrastructure model supports instruction, faculty research, and workforce development across the state and is provided to partner institutions at no cost.
To support the expanding use of artificial intelligence in teaching, research, and administrative functions, ITS launched a University -hosted AI platform based on LibreChat, deployed within a secure cloud environment.
The platform provides controlled acces s to multiple large language models hosted through

A-26 approved cloud providers and is designed to protect institutional and research data by isolating usage from public systems.
ITS has also deployed a secure version of Microsoft Copilot for all University faculty and staff, enabling productivity gains while maintaining institutional security and data governance standards.
Federal research sponsors increasingly require higher levels of data protection and compliance.
In response, ITS partnered with Hermathena Labs to provide secure research computing environments compliant with National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800- 171 and Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification requirements.
In parallel, the University is developing its own higher-security research enclave, known as Sanctuary, at MGHPCC.
Sanctuary is intended to provide a University -controlled environment for sensitive, regulated, and export -controlled research workloads, expanding long- term institutional capacity and reducing reliance on third-party platforms as resources permit.
Cybersecurity remains a significant and evolving challenge for higher education.

ITS has continued to strengthen the University’s security posture through expanded use of multi-factor authentication, enhanced network monitoring and intrusion prevention capabilities, and continued investment in disaster recovery and ransomware resilience.
These efforts are designed to reduce operational risk, protect sensitive information, and ensure continuity of academic and administrative services.
Despite these advances, ITS faces ongoing constraints related to staffing levels.
These constraints limit the pace at which new services can be expanded, legacy systems modernized, and emerging risks addressed.
As a result, certain enhancements in areas such as advanced security operations, expanded user support, and broader adoption of emerging technologies may require phased implementation over multiple years.
Through targeted investments and strategic partnerships, ITS supports student learning, faculty research, and institutional operations while managing risk and aligning technology capabilities with available resources and long-term University priorities.

FACILITIES The University’s current physical plant of 5. 7 million square feet across four campuses consists of 3 22 buildings (including leased buildings) including 24 residence halls, plus three apartment complexes and two dining centers, as well as the Memorial Union’s Ram’s Den.
Throughout its nearly continuous building program, the University has been successful in obtaining public financial support through the approval of bonds of the State issued for the benefit of the University for both renovation of older buildings and the construction of new buildings.
Over the last ten years, the University has completed more than $550 million in new construction and renovation and rehabilitation of existing structures.
Recent Completed Construction and Major Renovations: 2013 to 2024 Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center.
September 26, 2018 marked the official opening of the $8.2 million Robert J.
Higgins Welcome Center, funded by generous donors and one -time University funding sources.

Located on a prominent site on Upper College Road, this new state of the art building is an important tool for continuing the growth in applications which has enabled the University to increase enrollment significantly over the last ten years in the face of declining numbers of high school graduates nationally and regionally, while simultane ously increasing both the quality of the student body and its diversity.
The Higgins Welcome Center showcases URI students and their successes and enhances that all-important first impression for prospective students and families upon arrival at the Kingston Campus.
The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering (College of Engineering Phase I).
On October 7, 2019, the University dedicated The Fascitelli Center for Advanced Engineering, a new 187,000 square foot

A-27 building.
The phase 1 project started with the removal of five buildings that were built in the 1950s and 1960s to clear the site for the construction of the new building as well as renovation of the Kirk building.
The Fascitelli Center, funded by a generous donor as well as general obligation bonds issued by the State, comprises an east and west wing that are connected via what is effectively a truss bridge.
This center bridge manifests its structural members on the façade of the building, giving visual form to the engineering knowledge taught within which is in high demand by major employers in Rhode Island and serves as a draw to the State.
The College of Engineering Phase II project, which opened in January 2020, included the renovation of Bliss Hall and a new 15,000 square foot addition to the building.
This renovation restored the historic façade of Bliss Hall, home to the original College of Engineering when it opened in 1928 and established a new addition that architecturally linked Bliss Hall to The Fascitelli Center.
These projects were supported collectively by $150.5 million in voter approved general obligation bond support from the State.
Meade Stadium Artificial Tur f.

In 2019, the University of Rhode Island Athletic Department in conjunction with the Division of Student Affairs successfully completed the installation of an artificial surface and lights on Meade Stadium.
This project turned a facility that was used only six to eight times a year into one that can be used daily by URI’s varsity football program, along with general student use through intramurals and club sports.
This $4.1 million project, funded through $3 million of generous donor support and one-time Auxiliary Funding, was completed in time for the opening home football game on September 7, 2019.
Brookside Residence Hall.
The Brookside Residence Hall, an apartment-style residence hall on the west bank of the White Horn Brook on the Kingston campus, was dedicated on February 10, 2020.
This project is part of the University’s continuing initiative to provide safe, convenient, and affordable housing on the Kingston campus.
This state-of-the-art residence facility provides 500 new beds in an apartment-style six- story building focusing on upperclassmen.

In addition to providing safe and affordable housing, working with the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management, this project restored the section of White Horn Brook from Flagg Road to West Alumni Avenue, providing wildlife habitat, campus amenities, and stormwater improvements for this area of campus.
As an added amenity to the students living in Brookside and others on campus, this project provided the final northern connection to the campus bike path.
This bike path is now complete from Flagg Road heading south for approximately two miles to connect with the eight-mile William C.
O'Neill Bike Path that leads from the historic Kingston train station to the beaches in Narragansett.
Ranger Hall Phase II.
The Ranger Hall Phase II renovation was completed in August 2022.
This project built on the success of phase one, which opened in the fall of 2016 with the expansion of the Harrington School of Communication and Media to the second, third, and fourth floors of this historic building on the Kingston campus.

This renovation of the upper floors of Ranger Hall, funded by a generous private gift, provides the Harrington School with high technology classroom space to advance the Harrington School of Communication and Media as well as much needed general assignment classrooms in the heart of the academic core of the campus.
Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
In the fall of 2023, the University completed an $8.0 million privately fundraised renovation of the Soloviev Basketball Practice Facility.
This facility provides 24-hour access to state- of-the-art training facilities for URI’s highly competitive men's and women's basketball programs.
Infrastructure.
In the 2018 legislative session $19.8 million of much needed paving ($11 million), infrastructure ($6.5 million) and auxiliary fire protection ($2.3 million) projects were approved for revenue bond financing.
Working with RIHEBC these bonds have been issued in support of further improvements

A-28 of the campus’ hardscape, infrastructure and life safety needs.
To date $22.6 million (including interest and additional bond proceeds) has been expended out of these bond sources.
Phase Three of the University's progressive efforts to repave and reconstruct major pa rking facilities, internal roadways, walkways, and drainage systems across three of its four campuses has been completed.
The University has upgraded the high voltage electrical substations and electrical infrastructure on the Kingston Campus.
Work was completed on a new substation at Butterfield Road and an expanded substation on Flagg Road.
Improvements were made to the existing electrical system to support flexible back -feed capability throughout the system.
In 2024, the university began the installation of a centralized "generator farm" at the intersection of Butterfield and West Alumni Avenue to service the Roger Williams Complex residential buildings, and also conduct critical repairs to the steam line underneath the Hammerschlag Mall.
In addition, in 2023, Phase 2 of our Utility bond strategy was initiated.

In June of 2023, a bond for $15.44 million was issued and work has begun to improve our utility infrastructure systems on campus with this funding.
To date, we have spent $12.4 million.
Projects in Progress Narragansett Bay Campus Renewal – Phase I.
Leading an East Coast Oceanographic Consortium, the University of Rhode Island’s Graduate School of Oceanography in 2018 secured the management contract for a new, $125 million National Science Foundat ion (NSF) Regional Class Research Vessel, the Narraganset Dawn.
This vessel’s home base will be URI’s Narragansett Bay Campus.
To support this and other cutting-edge research that is ongoing at the Narragansett Bay Campus, in November 2018, Rhode Island voters approved $45 million of general obligation bonds of the State to support the project.
Phase IA of this project is the construction of a new, larger pier for the NSF research vessel.
The pier is substantially complete.Phase 1B of this project is to deliver the Ocean Robotics Laboratory, which will be completed in April 2026.
This building will bring together faculty from the Graduate School of Oceanography and the Ocean Engineering department.
